purpose: Further school-mock original core flashcard answer quality calibration across 65 Physics and Chemistry cards sampled independently from the source deck. One distinct correct alternative and two topic-specific incorrect misconceptions per unchanged original prompt and answer.
selection: AS first-mock Physics or taught Chemistry, unreviewed original source core cards with no original curated accepted/rejected lists. Exclude any ID already embedded in earlier app runtime patches.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is a systematic error?
records.originalBack: A consistent shift in readings caused by the method or instrument; repeats do not remove it.
accept: A systematic error biases readings consistently and is not eliminated by repeating measurements.
reject: It causes random scatter that averaging always removes.
It is a measurement error that changes sign unpredictably on every trial.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: If y = xⁿ, what happens to percentage uncertainty?
records.originalBack: Multiply the percentage uncertainty in x by |n|.
accept: For y equal to x to the power n, multiply the percentage uncertainty of x by the magnitude of n.
reject: Divide the percentage uncertainty by n regardless of the exponent.
The percentage uncertainty of x never changes when it is raised to a power.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Express the newton (N) using SI base units.
records.originalBack: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻², from F = ma.
accept: One newton equals one kilogram metre per second squared, kg m s^-2.
reject: A newton is kg m^2 s^-2.
A newton equals kg m s^-1.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Express the joule (J) using SI base units.
records.originalBack: 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻², because work done = force × distance.
accept: A joule is one kilogram metre squared per second squared, kg m^2 s^-2.
reject: A joule has the same SI dimensions as a newton.
A joule is kg m^2 s^-3.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Express the watt (W) using SI base units.
records.originalBack: 1 W = 1 kg m² s⁻³, because power = energy ÷ time.
accept: A watt is one kilogram metre squared per second cubed, kg m^2 s^-3.
reject: A watt is kg m^2 s^-2.
A watt is kg m s^-2.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is the principle of moments?
records.originalBack: In equilibrium, total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment.
accept: The clockwise and anticlockwise moments about a point balance for rotational equilibrium.
reject: In equilibrium the total clockwise moment is greater than anticlockwise moment.
The principle of moments requires the clockwise moments to be zero individually.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What does a negative velocity indicate?
records.originalBack: Motion opposite to the chosen positive direction.
accept: The object's velocity is directed opposite the chosen positive axis.
reject: Negative velocity means that the object must be slowing down.
Negative velocity always means that its acceleration is negative.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What does a negative acceleration mean?
records.originalBack: Acceleration opposite to the chosen positive direction.
accept: The acceleration vector is pointing in the negative reference direction.
reject: A negative acceleration always means decreasing speed.
Negative acceleration always indicates that velocity is negative.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Is deceleration always a negative acceleration?
records.originalBack: No; it depends on the chosen positive direction.
accept: No. Deceleration means decreasing speed, while the sign of acceleration depends on your chosen axis.
reject: Yes, deceleration always corresponds to an acceleration less than zero.
Deceleration can only happen while velocity is positive.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: How do you get total distance from a velocity–time graph?
records.originalBack: Add the magnitudes of all areas.
accept: Sum the absolute areas under every portion of the velocity-time graph.
reject: Add signed areas below the axis as negative distance.
Find total distance by taking only the gradient of the velocity-time graph.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What distance must be used in moment = force × distance?
records.originalBack: The perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force's line of action.
accept: Use the shortest perpendicular distance between the pivot and the line along which the force acts.
reject: Always use the length of the lever even if the force acts at an angle.
Use the distance measured parallel to the direction of the force.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: A spring force rises linearly 0→40 N during 0.50 m extension. Find energy stored.
records.originalBack: Area under F–extension = ½×40×0.50 = 10 J.
accept: Ten joules: the triangular area is one half multiplied by 40 N multiplied by 0.50 m.
reject: Twenty joules because energy is the rectangle 40 times 0.5.
Eighty joules because energy equals force divided by extension.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: A spring extends 0.060 m under 12 N within its Hooke's-law region. Find stiffness.
accept: Two hundred newtons per metre, from 12 divided by 0.060.
reject: 0.005 newtons per metre, from 0.060 divided by 12.
720 newtons per metre, from 12 times 0.060.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: A material retains extension after the force is removed. What behaviour has occurred?
records.originalBack: Plastic deformation: it has a permanent extension after unloading.
accept: Permanent deformation has occurred: the material has been plastically deformed.
reject: It is purely elastic deformation because it retains its extension.
The material must still obey Hooke's law perfectly after unloading.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: How does ductile failure typically differ from brittle failure?
records.originalBack: Ductile materials undergo substantial plastic deformation before breaking; brittle materials undergo little.
accept: A ductile solid shows considerable plastic extension before breaking, unlike a brittle solid.
reject: Brittle solids always have much greater plastic extension than ductile ones.
A ductile material breaks without undergoing any plastic deformation.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is a progressive wave?
records.originalBack: A travelling disturbance that transfers energy without net mass transfer.
accept: A progressive wave carries energy as a disturbance travels, without overall transport of the medium.
reject: A progressive wave carries the medium's particles along permanently with the wave.
A progressive wave cannot transfer energy.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is polarisation evidence for?
records.originalBack: Transverse oscillations.
accept: Polarisation shows that the wave has transverse oscillations.
reject: Polarisation proves the wave is longitudinal.
Polarisation is evidence that wave speed is zero.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Why can sound in air not be polarised?
records.originalBack: It is longitudinal.
accept: Sound waves in air have oscillations parallel to propagation, so they cannot be polarised.
reject: Sound in air is transverse and therefore polarises.
Sound waves are unpolarised because they do not carry energy.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: How does increasing string tension change wave speed?
records.originalBack: It increases, proportional to √tension.
accept: The speed rises with the square root of tension if mass per unit length stays fixed.
reject: Wave speed decreases in proportion to the square root of string tension.
Doubling tension always doubles wave speed.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is mass per unit length of a string?
records.originalBack: μ = mass/length, measured in kg m⁻¹.
accept: Mass per unit length is mu equals m divided by L, in kg per metre.
reject: The mass per unit length equals length divided by mass.
The unit of linear mass density is kg m.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What does coherent mean for two wave sources?
records.originalBack: Same frequency with constant phase difference.
accept: Coherent sources have equal frequencies and a constant phase difference.
reject: Coherent sources need only have the same amplitude.
Coherent sources have a phase difference that varies randomly.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Which colour spreads most in a white-light diffraction grating?
records.originalBack: Red; it has the longest wavelength.
accept: Red light is diffracted through the largest angle because its wavelength is greatest.
reject: Violet light always has the greatest diffraction angle in the same order.
All visible colours are diffracted through identical angles.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What happens to a single-slit central maximum when the slit narrows?
records.originalBack: It becomes wider.
accept: The central bright maximum becomes wider when a single slit is made narrower.
reject: The central bright maximum gets narrower as the slit narrows.
A narrower slit means no diffraction occurs.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is the highest possible order for a grating?
records.originalBack: The largest integer n with nλ ≤ d.
accept: The greatest possible order is the largest whole number no greater than d divided by wavelength.
reject: The greatest order is any integer larger than d divided by wavelength.
There is no limit to order even if n lambda exceeds d.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: In nuclide notation, what do A and Z mean?
records.originalBack: A = nucleon number; Z = proton number.
accept: A is the total number of protons and neutrons; Z is the proton number.
reject: A counts only the neutrons and Z counts all nucleons.
A is the proton number and Z is the neutron number.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is needed for pair production?
records.originalBack: A photon with enough energy creates a particle–antiparticle pair, usually near a nucleus to conserve momentum.
accept: A sufficiently energetic photon can create a particle-antiparticle pair near a nucleus to conserve momentum.
reject: Pair production means a particle and antiparticle turn into one photon.
Pair production creates a single charged particle without its antiparticle.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What are hadrons?
records.originalBack: Particles made of quarks that experience the strong interaction.
accept: Hadrons consist of quarks and take part in strong interactions.
reject: Hadrons are fundamental leptons made without quarks.
Hadrons do not experience the strong nuclear interaction.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is an ideal ammeter's resistance?
records.originalBack: Zero.
accept: An ideal ammeter has zero resistance, so it adds no voltage drop in series.
reject: An ideal ammeter has infinite resistance.
An ideal ammeter must be connected in parallel across the component.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What condition is required for Ohm's law?
records.originalBack: Constant physical conditions, including temperature.
accept: Ohm's law applies at constant physical conditions, particularly constant temperature.
reject: Ohm's law requires the resistor temperature to increase as the current rises.
Ohm's law applies only if the applied voltage stays at zero.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Why does a filament lamp's I–V curve flatten at high voltage?
records.originalBack: Its filament heats up and resistance rises.
accept: The hotter filament has higher resistance, so current rises less quickly as voltage increases.
reject: The filament cools as voltage rises and resistance falls.
The lamp's resistance remains constant at higher current.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Define relative atomic mass, Ar.
records.originalBack: Weighted mean mass of an atom relative to 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
accept: Ar is the abundance-weighted average atomic mass relative to one twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
reject: Ar is simply the mass number of the most abundant isotope, ignoring abundance.
Ar is the average atomic mass relative to one whole carbon-12 atom.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What are isotopes?
records.originalBack: Atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers.
accept: Isotopes share a proton number but contain different numbers of neutrons.
reject: Isotopes of an element have different proton numbers.
Isotopes have the same proton and neutron numbers but a different electron shell count.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is atom economy?
records.originalBack: Mr of desired product ÷ total Mr of reactants, accounting for coefficients, × 100.
accept: Atom economy is the desired product's formula mass divided by the sum of formula masses of reactants, with coefficients, times one hundred.
reject: Atom economy is the actual mass obtained divided by the theoretical yield.
Atom economy always equals the percentage yield.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is the formula for percentage yield?
records.originalBack: 100×actual yield/theoretical yield, using the same units.
accept: Percentage yield equals actual yield divided by theoretical yield multiplied by one hundred.
reject: Percentage yield equals theoretical yield divided by actual yield times one hundred.
Percentage yield equals desired product Mr divided by total reactant Mr.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is the difference between atom economy and percentage yield?
records.originalBack: Atom economy is theoretical atom distribution; yield compares actual and maximum product.
accept: Atom economy concerns theoretical destination of reactant atoms; percentage yield concerns actual versus theoretical product.
reject: Both atom economy and percentage yield are the same comparison of actual product to maximum product.
Atom economy measures how fast the reaction goes while yield measures equilibrium constant.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why is NaCl not made of separate NaCl molecules?
records.originalBack: The ions form a giant 3D lattice attracted in all directions.
accept: Sodium chloride forms an extended three-dimensional lattice of oppositely charged ions rather than distinct NaCl molecules.
reject: Each NaCl unit is a separate covalent molecule with a Na-Cl bond.
Solid NaCl consists of isolated ion pairs with no interactions beyond each pair.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is the formula of aluminium sulfate from Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻?
records.originalBack: Al₂(SO₄)₃: total charges +6 and −6 balance.
accept: Aluminium sulfate is Al2(SO4)3, balancing two aluminium 3+ ions with three sulfate 2- ions.
reject: The formula is AlSO4.
The formula is Al3(SO4)2.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Does a catalyst change a reaction's ΔH?
records.originalBack: No; it changes activation energy, not the initial/final enthalpy difference.
accept: Catalysts alter activation energy but not the enthalpy difference between products and reactants.
reject: A catalyst makes the reaction enthalpy more negative.
A catalyst changes the energy of the products without altering the reactants.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is an exothermic reaction?
records.originalBack: A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings; ΔH is negative.
accept: An exothermic reaction transfers heat to the surroundings and has a negative enthalpy change.
reject: Exothermic reactions take in heat and have positive delta H.
Exothermic reactions have zero enthalpy change.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is an endothermic reaction?
records.originalBack: A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings; ΔH is positive.
accept: An endothermic reaction takes in heat from the surroundings and has a positive enthalpy change.
reject: An endothermic reaction releases heat and has negative delta H.
An endothermic reaction cannot exchange thermal energy.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why are bond enthalpies usually positive?
records.originalBack: Energy is needed to break bonds.
accept: Bond-breaking requires energy input, hence bond dissociation enthalpies are positive.
reject: Breaking a bond always releases heat and has negative bond enthalpy.
Bond enthalpy is negative because new bonds always form simultaneously.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Which Group 2 sulfate is essentially insoluble?
records.originalBack: Barium sulfate, BaSO₄.
accept: Barium sulfate, BaSO4, is effectively insoluble.
reject: Magnesium sulfate is the least soluble Group 2 sulfate.
Barium sulfate dissolves readily in water.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What observation indicates sulfate ions in the barium-ion test?
records.originalBack: A white barium sulfate precipitate.
accept: Formation of a white precipitate of barium sulfate is the positive sulfate-ion observation.
reject: Sulfate gives a yellow silver iodide precipitate with barium ions.
The sulfate test is positive only when the solution remains clear.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why do halogen boiling points rise down the group?
records.originalBack: More electrons produce stronger van der Waals' forces.
accept: Larger halogen molecules have more electrons, making London dispersion forces stronger down the group.
reject: Boiling points rise because covalent bonds within halogen molecules become stronger.
London dispersion forces become weaker as electron count increases down Group 7.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: How does reducing strength of halide ions change down the group?
records.originalBack: It increases.
accept: Halide ions become stronger reducing agents down the group because they lose electrons more readily.
reject: Reducing strength decreases from chloride to iodide.
Halide ions cannot act as reducing agents.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What does zero order in A mean?
records.originalBack: Changing [A] does not change the rate; [A]⁰ = 1.
accept: For a zero-order reactant the rate is independent of its concentration.
reject: Zero order means doubling concentration doubles the rate.
Zero order means the reactant has a negative concentration.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What shape is the rate–[A] graph for second order?
records.originalBack: An upward-curving parabola: rate is proportional to [A]².
accept: For second order, rate is proportional to concentration squared, giving an upward-curved graph.
reject: Second order produces a horizontal straight line on a rate-versus-concentration graph.
Second order produces a straight line through the origin on a rate-versus-concentration graph.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What two conditions make a collision successful?
records.originalBack: Particles collide with energy at least equal to Ea and with a suitable orientation.
accept: A successful collision needs sufficient energy to overcome activation energy and a suitable orientation.
reject: Any collision is successful as long as particles have enough mass.
A collision is successful even with energy below activation energy.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: How does a catalyst increase reaction rate?
records.originalBack: It provides an alternative route with lower activation energy.
accept: A catalyst offers an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
reject: A catalyst increases reaction rate by increasing activation energy.
A catalyst speeds a reaction by changing equilibrium enthalpy.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What must all mole fractions in a gas mixture add up to?
records.originalBack: Exactly 1, when all gases present are included.
accept: The mole fractions of every gas present add up to one.
reject: All gas mole fractions must add up to the total pressure.
All mole fractions in a gas mixture add up to zero.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is first electron affinity?
records.originalBack: Enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms each gains one electron to form gaseous 1− ions.
accept: First electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms each gains one electron to form gaseous 1- ions.
reject: First electron affinity involves removal of electrons from gaseous atoms.
First electron affinity is defined for atoms in the solid state gaining electrons.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is the condition for thermodynamic feasibility using Gibbs free energy?
records.originalBack: ΔG < 0 at the stated temperature.
accept: Negative Gibbs free energy change, delta G less than zero, indicates thermodynamic feasibility in the forward direction.
reject: A positive delta G always guarantees spontaneous forward reaction.
A negative activation energy is the criterion for thermodynamic feasibility.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Does thermodynamic feasibility guarantee a fast reaction?
records.originalBack: No; kinetic barriers can make it slow.
accept: No. A negative Gibbs change is compatible with a high activation energy and a very slow reaction.
reject: Every thermodynamically feasible reaction must be fast.
Thermodynamic feasibility eliminates any kinetic barrier.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is a conjugate acid–base pair?
records.originalBack: Two species differing by one proton.
accept: A conjugate acid-base pair differs by one hydrogen ion, H+.
reject: A conjugate acid-base pair differs by one electron.
A conjugate acid-base pair must contain two unrelated substances with the same pH.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Which haloalkane reacts fastest in hydrolysis: fluoro or iodo?
records.originalBack: Iodoalkane, because its C–I bond is weaker.
accept: Iodoalkanes hydrolyse more quickly because the carbon-iodine bond is weaker than carbon-fluorine.
reject: Fluoroalkanes hydrolyse faster because the C-F bond is easiest to break.
Both haloalkanes have identical hydrolysis rates because all C-halogen bonds have identical strength.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is the organic product type from substitution by CN⁻?
records.originalBack: A nitrile.
accept: Nucleophilic substitution by cyanide forms a nitrile containing the -C triple bond N group.
reject: Substitution by cyanide gives an aldehyde as the main product.
Substitution by cyanide produces a haloalkane containing -COOH.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What does oxidising a primary alcohol first produce?
records.originalBack: An aldehyde.
accept: A primary alcohol is first oxidised to an aldehyde.
reject: Oxidising a primary alcohol initially produces a ketone.
Primary alcohols are not oxidisable under normal laboratory conditions.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why are tertiary alcohols resistant to normal oxidation?
records.originalBack: No hydrogen on the carbon attached to –OH.
accept: Tertiary alcohols lack a hydrogen on the carbon bearing the OH group, so ordinary oxidation does not occur.
reject: Tertiary alcohols oxidise most easily because they have three carbon groups.
They resist oxidation because the OH group is absent.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is a racemic mixture?
records.originalBack: Equal amounts of two enantiomers.
accept: A racemic mixture has equal quantities of the two enantiomers.
reject: A racemic mixture contains only one enantiomer.
A racemic mixture always has a 90:10 ratio of enantiomers.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Where do the C=O bonding electrons move during nucleophilic addition?
records.originalBack: Towards oxygen while the incoming group bonds to carbon.
accept: The carbonyl pi-electron pair moves onto the oxygen as the nucleophile bonds to carbon.
reject: The C=O bonding electron pair moves onto carbon while the nucleophile attaches to oxygen.
The carbonyl oxygen donates its lone pair to form a new C=O triple bond.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Which carbonyl compound gives a positive Tollens' test?
records.originalBack: An aldehyde.
accept: An aldehyde gives a positive Tollens' silver mirror test.
reject: Ketones always give Tollens' silver mirror test, whereas aldehydes never do.
All carbonyl compounds always give a positive Tollens' result.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is esterification?
records.originalBack: Formation of an ester from a carboxylic acid and alcohol.
accept: Esterification joins an alcohol and a carboxylic acid to form an ester and water.
reject: Esterification is addition of water to cleave an ester.
Esterification forms an amide directly from two alcohols.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why does alkaline ester hydrolysis tend to completion?
records.originalBack: Formation of the stable carboxylate ion inhibits the reverse reaction.
accept: Base hydrolysis tends to go to completion because a carboxylate ion forms, making reverse esterification unfavourable.
reject: Alkaline hydrolysis remains fully reversible because the carboxylate ion is readily protonated by the base.
Alkaline hydrolysis is driven to completion because all products are gases.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: How should a colourless liquid meniscus be read?
records.originalBack: At eye level, using the bottom of the meniscus.
accept: Read the bottom of the colourless meniscus level with your eyes to avoid parallax.
reject: Read the upper edge of the colourless meniscus from above.
Read a colourless meniscus from well below eye level for accuracy.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What does a racemic mixture do to plane-polarised light?
records.originalBack: Produces no net rotation.
accept: Equal and opposite optical rotations cancel, so a racemate gives no net rotation of plane-polarised light.
reject: A racemate rotates plane-polarised light twice as much as a pure enantiomer.
Both enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light in the same direction.

limitations: 65 targeted card edits do not certify full AQA bullet coverage or perfection of unseen typed answers.
Card prompts and model answers remain unchanged; multiple-skill source cards remain a separate editorial concern.
Saved card IDs, mock selectors and local/cloud progress are untouched.
